name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANATOMYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_AR_Q01 - Absence of cuticle in plant roots

questiontext.text:
Assertion (A): The cuticle is completely absent on the epidermal surface of roots.

Reason (R): The root epidermis is specialized for the absorption of water and minerals from the soil, a function that would be obstructed by a water-impermeable waxy layer.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Evaluation of the Assertion
The epidermis of roots, termed epiblema, lacks a waxy cuticle covering. Hence, the assertion stating that the cuticle is completely absent on the epidermal surface of roots is correct.

Step 2: Evaluation of the Reason
Cuticle is a waxy layer designed to prevent water loss. Because root epidermal cells must freely take up water and dissolved minerals from the soil moisture, having a waterproof cuticle would prevent absorption. Hence, the reason is correct.

Step 3: Evaluation of the Relationship
The necessity of unhindered water absorption directly accounts for why root epidermal cells do not develop a protective waxy cuticle. Thus, the reason correctly explains the assertion.

Final Answer:
Both the assertion and the reason are correct, and the reason is the correct explanation of the assertion.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANATOMYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_AR_Q02 - Dumbbell shaped guard cells in grasses

questiontext.text:
Assertion (A): In grasses, the guard cells enclosing the stomatal pore are dumb-bell shaped rather than bean-shaped.

Reason (R): Dumb-bell shaped guard cells lack chloroplasts and do not participate in regulating stomatal opening and closing.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Evaluation of the Assertion
In monocotyledonous grasses, the guard cells enclosing the stomatal aperture are characteristically dumb-bell shaped, whereas typical dicots possess bean-shaped guard cells. Hence, the assertion is correct.

Step 2: Evaluation of the Reason
Guard cells in all flowering plants, including grasses, possess chloroplasts and actively regulate the opening and closing of the stomatal aperture through turgor adjustments. Hence, the reason is incorrect.

Final Answer:
The assertion is correct, but the reason is incorrect.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANATOMYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_AR_Q03 - Open vascular bundles in dicot stems

questiontext.text:
Assertion (A): Vascular bundles in dicotyledonous stems are classified as open vascular bundles.

Reason (R): A strip of intrafascicular cambium is present between the xylem and phloem, granting the bundles the capacity to form secondary tissues.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Evaluation of the Assertion
In dicot stems, vascular bundles are designated as open bundles because they are capable of undergoing secondary growth. Hence, the assertion is correct.

Step 2: Evaluation of the Reason
The presence of a lateral meristematic tissue (cambium) situated between primary xylem and primary phloem provides the developmental potential to produce secondary xylem and secondary phloem. Hence, the reason is correct.

Step 3: Evaluation of the Relationship
The presence of cambium between xylem and phloem is the precise anatomical defining feature that makes a vascular bundle open. Thus, the reason is the correct explanation of the assertion.

Final Answer:
Both the assertion and the reason are correct, and the reason is the correct explanation of the assertion.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANATOMYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_AR_Q04 - Differential wall thickening in guard cells

questiontext.text:
Assertion (A): The inner walls of guard cells facing the stomatal pore are highly thickened, whereas their outer walls away from the pore are thin.

Reason (R): The stomatal aperture, guard cells, and surrounding subsidiary cells together constitute the stomatal apparatus.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Evaluation of the Assertion
In stomatal guard cells, the outer wall directed away from the pore is thin and extensible, while the inner wall directed towards the pore is conspicuously thickened. This differential thickening facilitates stomatal opening upon turgor increase. Hence, the assertion is correct.

Step 2: Evaluation of the Reason
By anatomical definition, the stomatal aperture, the pair of guard cells, and the adjacent specialized subsidiary cells collectively form the stomatal apparatus. Hence, the reason is correct.

Step 3: Evaluation of the Relationship
The definition of the stomatal apparatus does not explain why the inner and outer walls of guard cells develop unequal wall thicknesses. Thus, the reason is not the correct explanation of the assertion.

Final Answer:
Both the assertion and the reason are correct, but the reason is not the correct explanation of the assertion.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANATOMYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_AR_Q05 - Closed vascular bundles in monocot stems

questiontext.text:
Assertion (A): Vascular bundles of monocotyledonous stems are described as closed and do not undergo secondary growth.

Reason (R): Monocotyledonous vascular bundles possess a persistent layer of vascular cambium between protoxylem and metaxylem.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Evaluation of the Assertion
In monocotyledonous stems, vascular bundles lack cambium and do not produce secondary vascular tissues, so they are referred to as closed vascular bundles. Hence, the assertion is correct.

Step 2: Evaluation of the Reason
Monocot vascular bundles are completely devoid of intrafascicular cambium; no meristematic strip exists between the xylem and phloem. Hence, the reason is incorrect.

Final Answer:
The assertion is correct, but the reason is incorrect.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANATOMYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_AR_Q06 - Comparison between root hairs and trichomes

questiontext.text:
Assertion (A): Root hairs are multicellular elongations of epidermal cells that help prevent water loss due to transpiration.

Reason (R): Trichomes present on the shoot system are usually multicellular epidermal appendages that help prevent transpiration water loss.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Evaluation of the Assertion
Root hairs are unicellular (not multicellular) tubular projections of root epiblema cells, and their physiological role is the absorption of water and minerals from the soil, not prevention of transpirational water loss. Hence, the assertion is incorrect.

Step 2: Evaluation of the Reason
Epidermal hairs on the stem, termed trichomes, are typically multicellular, can be branched or unbranched, and function to reduce air movement across the surface, thereby helping prevent water loss from transpiration. Hence, the reason is correct.

Final Answer:
The assertion is incorrect, but the reason is correct.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANATOMYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_AR_Q07 - Role of bulliform cells in grasses

questiontext.text:
Assertion (A): In grasses, leaves curl inwards during periods of severe water stress to minimize water loss.

Reason (R): When bulliform cells lose water and become flaccid due to water deficit, they cause the leaf lamina to roll inwards.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Evaluation of the Assertion
Grasses exhibit inward rolling of their leaf blades when exposed to drought or dry conditions, which protects the stomatal surface and restricts transpiration. Hence, the assertion is correct.

Step 2: Evaluation of the Reason
Bulliform cells are large, thin-walled, empty epidermal cells along veins. When turgid, they keep the leaf blade expanded; when they lose water under drought stress and turn flaccid, the mechanical tension curls the leaf inward. Hence, the reason is correct.

Step 3: Evaluation of the Relationship
The loss of turgidity in bulliform cells provides the direct mechanical drive for the inward curling of the grass leaf blade. Thus, the reason correctly explains the assertion.

Final Answer:
Both the assertion and the reason are correct, and the reason is the correct explanation of the assertion.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANATOMYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_AR_Q08 - Starch sheath identity in dicot stems

questiontext.text:
Assertion (A): In a primary dicotyledonous stem, the endodermis is also referred to as the starch sheath.

Reason (R): The hypodermis of a dicotyledonous stem is composed of collenchymatous cells that provide mechanical strength to the young stem.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Evaluation of the Assertion
The innermost layer of the cortex in a dicot stem is the endodermis, whose cells are rich in starch grains, earning it the designation of starch sheath. Hence, the assertion is correct.

Step 2: Evaluation of the Reason
The outermost cortical zone situated beneath the epidermis in a young dicot stem consists of a few collenchyma layers that grant mechanical support to growing shoot tissues. Hence, the reason is correct.

Step 3: Evaluation of the Relationship
The presence and mechanical role of collenchyma in the hypodermis does not account for why the separate, innermost endodermal layer is named the starch sheath (which is due to starch grain accumulation). Thus, the reason is not the correct explanation of the assertion.

Final Answer:
Both the assertion and the reason are correct, but the reason is not the correct explanation of the assertion.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANATOMYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_AR_Q09 - Vascular bundle sizes in monocot stem

questiontext.text:
Assertion (A): In the transverse section of a monocotyledonous stem, peripheral vascular bundles are generally smaller than centrally located ones.

Reason (R): Water-containing cavities are typically present within the vascular bundles of monocotyledonous stems.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Evaluation of the Assertion
In monocot stems, vascular bundles are scattered throughout the ground tissue, with smaller, more densely packed bundles situated near the periphery and larger bundles situated towards the center. Hence, the assertion is correct.

Step 2: Evaluation of the Reason
The vascular bundles of monocot stems feature lysigenous water-containing cavities formed by the breakdown of protoxylem elements during stem elongation. Hence, the reason is correct.

Step 3: Evaluation of the Relationship
The presence of protoxylem water lacunae within vascular bundles is an internal structural feature of each bundle and does not explain the spatial size gradient between peripheral and central bundles. Thus, the reason is not the correct explanation of the assertion.

Final Answer:
Both the assertion and the reason are correct, but the reason is not the correct explanation of the assertion.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANATOMYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_AR_Q10 - Suberin deposition in root Casparian strips

questiontext.text:
Assertion (A): Casparian strips in the root endodermis allow free apoplastic diffusion of water and dissolved minerals into the stele.

Reason (R): The tangential as well as radial walls of root endodermal cells possess a deposition of water-impermeable, waxy material suberin.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Evaluation of the Assertion
Casparian strips form an impermeable barrier in the endodermis that blocks the apoplastic movement of water, forcing solutes and water to traverse the selectively permeable plasma membranes (symplastic pathway). Hence, the assertion stating that Casparian strips allow free apoplastic diffusion is incorrect.

Step 2: Evaluation of the Reason
The defining anatomical hallmark of the root endodermis is the presence of Casparian strips, which consist of waxy suberin deposited along both the tangential and radial cell walls. Hence, the reason is correct.

Final Answer:
The assertion is incorrect, but the reason is correct.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANATOMYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_AR_Q11 - Parallel venation effect in isobilateral leaves

questiontext.text:
Assertion (A): In vertical sections of an isobilateral leaf, the vascular bundles appear nearly similar in size, except in the main veins.

Reason (R): Isobilateral leaves possess a reticulate venation system in which veins branch repeatedly into veinlets of highly divergent diameters.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Evaluation of the Assertion
In monocotyledonous (isobilateral) leaves, cross sections reveal vascular bundles of nearly identical dimensions, with only the primary central veins being substantially larger. Hence, the assertion is correct.

Step 2: Evaluation of the Reason
Monocot leaves display parallel venation, where veins run alongside each other at uniform thickness, whereas reticulate venation is characteristic of dicot leaves. Hence, the reason is incorrect.

Final Answer:
The assertion is correct, but the reason is incorrect.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANATOMYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_AR_Q12 - Pericycle role in lateral root initiation

questiontext.text:
Assertion (A): In primary dicotyledonous roots, lateral roots originate exogenously from the cortical parenchyma cells.

Reason (R): In dicot roots, the pericycle consists of thick-walled parenchymatous cells that initiate lateral roots and vascular cambium during secondary growth.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Evaluation of the Assertion
In flowering plants, lateral roots originate endogenously from the pericycle layers situated deep inside the endodermis, rather than exogenously from outer cortical cells. Hence, the assertion is incorrect.

Step 2: Evaluation of the Reason
The pericycle in dicot roots is composed of a few layers of thick-walled parenchyma cells, and these cells retain the meristematic potential to give rise to lateral root primordia as well as part of the secondary vascular cambium. Hence, the reason is correct.

Final Answer:
The assertion is incorrect, but the reason is correct.
